title: Mosquitoes are a choice - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Works in Progress argues the US could eliminate mosquito-borne disease now, since Oxitec's gene-suppression mosquitoes and Wolbachia releases cut populations 80-95% and dengue by about 70%, but regulation is the bottleneck. Oxitec spent a decade bouncing between the USDA, FDA and EPA and is still unregistered, while non-GM Wolbachia (MosquitoMate) won registration in 2024; the fix proposed is EPA capacity built on FDA-style user fees.

themes.theme: Mosquito-borne disease returning to the US

insights.claim: US dengue cases hit almost 4,000 in 2024, a 360% rise over the prior-decade average of 830 per year, with locally acquired transmission in Florida, California and Texas and ten locally acquired malaria cases in 2023, the first in twenty years; warming and pesticide resistance are driving the return.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Vector-borne disease is becoming a domestic public-health and cost issue, raising demand for vector-control tech and exposing regions in the Sun Belt.
insights.quote: In 2024, the country reported almost 4,000 cases of dengue, a 360 percent increase over the average of 830 per year over the previous decade
insights.locator: Most Americans think of mosquito-borne diseases

insights.claim: The US is wealthy enough, and its disease-carrying mosquito population small enough, that it could eliminate mosquito-borne disease within its borders; the binding constraint is regulation, not technology.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Value in vector-control tech is gated by approval timelines, so regulatory milestones are the key catalyst to track.
insights.quote: The reason we haven’t is that the technology has spent fifteen years in regulatory limbo.
insights.locator: But we don’t have to accept this threat

themes.theme: Genetic suppression and the sterile insect precedent

insights.claim: Oxitec's engineered male Aedes aegypti pass a tetracycline-repressed lethal gene that kills female offspring; the effect is self-limiting over a few generations, and field trials cut wild populations about 80% in the Cayman Islands and about 95% in Juazeiro, Brazil.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The technology has strong efficacy evidence; the self-limiting design is a built-in containment argument for regulators.
insights.quote: Sustained releases cut a wild Aedes aegypti population in the Cayman Islands by 80 percent

insights.claim: The USDA's radiation-based sterile insect technique cleared screwworm from the US in the 1960s, saving cattle farmers close to $800 million per year, but containment broke and Texas detected the first US case in 60 years in June 2026, likely via cattle smuggling from Central America.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Pest-control capability erodes when programs lapse; livestock and agricultural-input exposure to screwworm is now a live risk, with sterile-fly capacity a bottleneck.
insights.quote: Texas detected the United States’ first case of screwworm in 60 years

insights.claim: Sterile-insect releases have also held back the Mediterranean fruit fly, where resettlement in California could cost over a billion dollars per year in crop damage, showing the economic payoff of mass insect release.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Mass-release biocontrol has a proven cost-benefit record that strengthens the case for mosquito programs.

themes.theme: Regulatory ping-pong delayed Oxitec a decade

insights.claim: Oxitec was bounced across three agencies: the USDA took 18 months to reject its 2010 application, the FDA held it five years before carving out mosquito population control, and the EPA granted only an Experimental Use Permit in May 2020, a decade after the first filing.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Jurisdictional ambiguity is the main cost driver for novel biotech; time-to-market for new categories should be modelled in years not months.
insights.quote: In its third review, at the EPA, Oxitec’s mosquitoes were subject to the rules governing pesticides

insights.claim: Oxitec's permit expired in April 2024 and full commercial registration is still pending two years later; the scientific advisory panel planned for November 2025 was postponed with no new date, and a 2022 release of up to 2.4 billion mosquitoes was paused after public pushback.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Oxitec has no US commercial path near term; public opposition compounds regulatory risk for gene-edited organisms.
insights.quote: Their full registration remains pending, over two years after the end of their field trial permit.

insights.claim: Because Wolbachia is a natural bacterium and involves no genetic modification, it could bypass the regulation that stalled Oxitec; released infected males cause non-hatching eggs, and released infected females seed populations with virus resistance.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Non-GM approaches to the same biological outcome can win the race to market; regulatory classification can matter more than technical superiority.
insights.quote: since this approach does not involve genetic modification, it ought to be able to bypass much of the regulation

insights.claim: A randomized Singapore trial of Wolbachia-infected male releases cut mosquito populations 85% versus control and dengue infections about 70%.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: City-scale randomized evidence supports demand from municipal mosquito control districts.
insights.quote: releases of Wolbachia-infected males cut mosquito populations by 85 percent compared to control areas and dengue infections by roughly 70 percent

insights.claim: MosquitoMate won full nationwide registration as the first live mosquito biopesticide in April 2024, fifteen years after the Wolbachia breakthrough; the Florida Keys adopted it in 2025 and the San Gabriel Valley in 2026.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A commercial beachhead exists, with local districts as the customer base; adoption is spreading district by district.

insights.claim: Google's Debug requested EPA approval in June 2026 to release 64 million Wolbachia mosquitoes in California and Florida, targeting Culex quinquefasciatus for West Nile virus, yet must restart the Experimental Use Permit process despite the same underlying technology.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Big-tech entry signals capital and scale arriving; per-species re-review is a recurring friction that delays each new target.
insights.quote: it must complete the Experimental Use Permit process from the beginning

themes.theme: Biotech regulation has not kept pace

insights.claim: No major new US biotech regulation has passed since the 1980s; the 1986 Coordinated Framework still divides jurisdiction by categories designed for the previous century, leaving unclear which agency oversees new products, as with cell-cultured meat until Congress forced a split.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Novel biotech categories face multi-year jurisdictional delays; reform or congressional action is the catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: the regulation that governs the use of these new technologies hasn’t kept pace

insights.claim: Biden's 2022 executive order told agencies to resolve regulatory uncertainties and update the Coordinated Framework, but almost none of it happened and Trump rescinded the order in March 2025.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Executive-order-driven harmonization is fragile across administrations, so durable change likely needs legislation.
insights.quote: But almost none of it happened; President Trump rescinded the order in March 2025

insights.claim: The EPA's Vector Expedited Review Voucher, introduced in 2022, rewards firms that register a novel mosquito product with faster review of their next application, but does nothing about the underlying backlog; the responsible EPA unit is small and uses pesticide protocols that ill-fit dispersal and inheritance questions.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Incentive vouchers help early movers but capacity, not priority, is the bottleneck.
insights.quote: it doesn’t do anything about the long regulatory backlog itself

themes.theme: User-fee funding as the fix for review capacity

insights.claim: The 1992 Prescription Drug User Fee Act shifted two thirds of FDA human-drug review funding to industry fees, cutting median review from 29 months in the late 1980s to targets of ten months standard and six priority, met in most cases; each 100 added reviewers cut review time by about 3.3 months.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Fee-funded staffing is a proven way to compress approval timelines; an analogous EPA scheme would be a catalyst for biopesticide and biotech pipelines.
insights.quote: review times fell by roughly 3.3 months for every 100 reviewers the FDA added

insights.claim: The EPA gets two thirds of its budget from Congress and only one third from fees, which leaves it more dependent on appropriations and less able to scale review capacity than the FDA.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Appropriation-dependent agencies are likely to remain slow; user-fee legislation for EPA is the structural lever.
insights.quote: The EPA, by contrast, is much more reliant on congressional appropriation

insights.claim: Mosquito-borne disease in the US is now a policy choice: technologies to eliminate it exist, so continued cases reflect regulatory inertia rather than scientific limits.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Policy change on review speed could unlock a step-change in adoption, making regulation the key variable for vector-control investments.
insights.quote: New technologies mean that mosquito-borne disease is now a choice in the United States.
insights.locator: It shouldn’t have to take fifteen years
